summary: Grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery are the practical uses; governance capacity is the constraint. No single entity keeps a real-time registry of nonprofit AI adoption - coverage comes from sector research organizations, and this page names the ones that actually publish it.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use among firms in NAICS 81, Other services, which includes grantmaking and civic organizations, at 13.7% in the latest reading, up from 12.6% in the prior period. The question asks whether the business used AI in the last two weeks, so this is a narrow, recent-use measure rather than a broad adoption claim. It is the only hard adoption figure available for the sector, and it suggests AI remains a minority practice among the organizations the category covers.

What the sources describe is a sector where AI is being considered mainly for administrative work rather than programmatic decision-making. Per Candid, nearly a quarter of corporate funders support using AI to decide grant approvals and denials, but for most, using AI for administrative tasks will free up time. The Center for Effective Philanthropy's research examines how foundations and nonprofits use AI for operations, program delivery, and communications, and this site's coverage of the sector points to grant writing, donor analytics, and service delivery on small budgets as the practical use cases.

The vendor and organizational landscape is thin. The World of AI catalogs four individually verified organizations in its nonprofits and open source foundations category: two nonprofits and two open-source foundations. LMSYS stewards Chatbot Arena, a neutral evaluation platform, while Khan Academy is an end-user of AI in education, and the Krita Foundation and Blender Foundation steward creative tools that intersect with AI-generated content. The catalog notes explicitly that none are infrastructure builders in the compute or power sense, and that there are no training compute providers, no standards bodies, and no open-model foundations releasing weights for public use. Candid tracks the funding side, including grantmaking directed toward AI adoption and technology infrastructure, but the excerpts do not quantify that flow.

Access and equity are recurring themes. The AI Equity Project builds structured learning pathways and intergenerational programs, transforms public libraries and community spaces into interactive learning environments, and operates as a global network providing standardized technical curricula and training assets to underrepresented communities. NTEN states that nonprofit technology is marked by inequities within organizations and the sector that must be dismantled, and it runs sector-wide research on technology investment, digital maturity, and AI policy adoption among nonprofits.

On governance, Stanford HAI's AI Index reports a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, with frameworks needed to govern, evaluate, and understand the technology falling behind and data transparency declining. That macro finding lands directly on a sector where governance capacity is identified as the binding constraint. A reader deciding whether to deploy should take from this that measured adoption is modest, that funders mostly see AI as an administrative time-saver rather than a grantmaking decision-maker, that the nonprofit AI vendor ecosystem is small and not infrastructure-grade, and that equity and governance questions are the ones the sector's own institutions keep raising.

https://cep.org/.brief: The Center for Effective Philanthropy page announces a limited-time discount on 2027 assessments or advisory projects, with savings up to $1000 for signing up before Sept. 30. It promotes a podcast episode where donors Jeff Atwood and Dr. Betsy Burton discuss their commitment to give away $50 million in five years. CEP describes its work offering assessments, data-driven research, customized advisory services, events, and blog commentary to influence foundations and major donors. The page also highlights new data on how nonprofits are faring and how foundations are responding, and features blog posts on topics such as inflation’s impact on grantmaking and deciding when a foundation’s mission requires more spending.

https://candid.org/.brief: Candid offers a large database of grants and nonprofit information to help users locate funding opportunities, research organizations, and connect with funders. According to Candid, about 25 % of corporate funders use AI to decide grant approvals and denials. For most funders, Candid reports that “using AI for administrative tasks will free up time.” The site emphasizes its comprehensive data as a resource for those seeking funding or researching nonprofits.

https://www.nten.org/.brief: NTEN presents itself as a nonprofit community focused on using technology for social change. It offers networking opportunities, job listings, and professional development resources such as certificates and scholarships. Members can pledge to use an Equity Guide and support open-source developers. NTEN also encourages participation in committees on accessibility, equity, and programs.

https://theaiequityproject.org/.brief: The AI Equity Project reports that it develops structured educational routes and cross-generational initiatives aimed at making AI usable, ethical, and practical for every community. It says it converts public libraries and local community venues into hands-on learning settings where older adults and student volunteers jointly try out practical AI tools. The organization also describes a worldwide network that supplies standardized technical curricula and training materials to underrepresented groups, with support structures meant to ensure each student directly helps deploy machine learning architectures. Its International AI for Impact Challenge asks engineering candidates to propose operational algorithms for real-world issues, and top entrants receive engineering lab partnerships, academic research access, and intellectual property advice.

https://theworldofai.org/ai-ecosystem/ec.brief: The page reports that four organizations, two nonprofits and two open-source foundations, steer AI tools and evaluation infrastructure, but none build compute infrastructure. LMSYS manages the “Chatbot Arena” platform, a neutral evaluation tool used by the AI community to benchmark model quality. Khan Academy applies AI in education, while the Krita and Blender Foundations maintain creative software that increasingly intersects with AI-generated imagery and 3D content. The page notes it does not cover training compute providers, standards bodies, or open-model foundations, and that the information is limited to organizational structure and nonprofit status, offering no insight into funding or governance.
